title: Remembering death
hookLine: remember often the destroyer of pleasures, said the Prophet; and a week of home, elders and the sick ends here

lines: WHY THINK OF DEATH ON PURPOSE?
cards: Why would anyone think about death on purpose? In a hadith kept by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says something that would sound almost rude at a party.
Remember often, he said, the destroyer of pleasures. He meant death. Not as a threat.

As a remembering, brought to mind in the middle of ordinary life: a good meal, a long laugh with friends, a new thing finally in your hands. This week walked from the home, to the elders, to the sickbed.
Today it reaches the place every one of those roads ends.

teach.h: EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.
teach.b: The Qur'an says it plainly, in Pickthall's translation of surah Al 'Imran: "Every soul will taste of death." No exceptions in the sentence. So what is the remembering for?

The hadith gives one clue in its own wording: it destroys pleasures. Some readers take that not as ruining every good thing, but as cutting through the ones that have grown too large. The argument you're still nursing.
The thing you'd do anything to own.

teach.h: IT SHRINKS THINGS BACK TO SIZE.
teach.b: Death, remembered for a moment, shrinks them back to size. Another hadith, in al-Bukhari, gives the posture.
The Prophet took 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar by the shoulder and told him, in paraphrase: be in this world as though you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through.

And Ibn 'Umar used to say: when evening comes, don't wait for the morning, and when morning comes, don't wait for the evening. A traveler doesn't hate the road. A traveler just doesn't unpack everything.
Now look back over this week through that lens. Serving at home, in 'A'ishah's report. Tending the flock you were given.
The gracious word to the old. The visit to the sick. The patience in the hard hours.
Each of those is something a traveler would want done before the road ends. Remembering death, in this teaching, isn't gloom.

teach.h: IT MAKES THE SMALL KINDNESS URGENT.
teach.b: It's what makes today's small kindness urgent.

how: Muslims are encouraged to remember death often, citing the hadith of the destroyer of pleasures and the Qur'an's "Every soul will taste of death"; some visit graves for this reason.

o: visiting graves once a year on a set day of mourning
bringing death to mind on purpose, so small things shrink
dwelling on fear of death so you stop enjoying anything

p: every soul will taste of death

s: in this teaching, remembering death is meant to make life gloomy
it shrinks the overgrown things and makes the good ones urgent.
the hadith says to remember the destroyer of pleasures often
Ibn 'Umar was told to be in this world as a stranger or a traveler
the Prophet took him by the shoulder and said it, in al-Bukhari.

games.q: you're a traveler passing through a town. what do you do with your bags?
o: keep them ready; you're passing through.
games.why: be in this world as a stranger or a traveler, in al-Bukhari: not hating the road, just not unpacking everything.

practice: Without drama, let yourself remember that this life has an end, as every life does, and stay with that gently for a few breaths.
Then ask: if the road were shorter than I think, what from this week would I want to have done, a visit, a call, an apology, a job at home? If you pray, turn that answer into your prayer.
And if thoughts of death ever feel heavy or close, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Remembering death. Bringing the end to mind on purpose, often, so the small things shrink and the good ones get done. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the end. A traveler on the road doesn't unpack everything. That's the week, and thank you for walking it.
